waypoints.name: Duckabush Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee required at this vault-toilet trailhead; overnight parties need an Olympic NP wilderness permit once the trail crosses the park boundary.

waypoints.name: Five Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Established riverside camp along the Duckabush River Trail; reliable river water, treat before drinking.

waypoints.name: Ten Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Last established campsite before the trail turns south for La Crosse Pass; sits at 1,400 ft with river water nearby.

waypoints.name: La Crosse Pass Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Duckabush River Trail forks here onto the La Crosse Pass Trail, which immediately switchbacks steeply up the valley wall toward the pass.

waypoints.name: La Crosse Pass
waypoints.note: No water at the pass (dry for miles either direction); leave the maintained trail here and start the cross-country climb north across heather and talus toward the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount La Crosse
waypoints.note: True summit reached via open heather benches and talus on the broad ridge crest, Class 2-3; best climbed June-September before snow returns.

approach_variants.name: Duckabush River Trail to La Crosse Pass
approach_variants.notes: A long valley walk to the La Crosse Pass junction, then a steep switchbacking climb of roughly three thousand feet in about a mile to the pass — loose and eroded in places and considerably harder coming down on tired legs. The West Fork Dosewallips reaches the same pass on a gentler grade and is the kinder exit if you are through-hiking.
hazards: No water at the pass or above it — carry from a creek far below
Open, sparsely cairned country that is easy to lose in fog
Snow on north-facing slopes and gullies into early July
Loose talus that is more hazardous descending than climbing
Bear canisters required and a self-rescue distance measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding: La Crosse Pass is a bald, waterless saddle on the Duckabush–Dosewallips divide, with maintained trail crossing it and dropping steeply away on both sides — there is nothing else like it for miles and you cannot arrive at it by accident. Leave the tread at the top of the pass and head north onto open heather and talus. There is no gully mouth or rock step to find here: the climb begins straight off the trail, so the thing to identify is the correct ridge rather than a base. The line is the broad crest running north out of the saddle, and once the heather benches give way to talus that crest is the handrail all the way to the top. Two things pull people the wrong way. White Mountain stands less than a mile southwest and is the more obvious summit from the pass. And the Anderson massif filling the northern skyline is much further off than it looks, so do not use it as your aiming point. In early summer lingering snowfields bury the ground around the pass and the tread is routinely lost on the way back down — take a bearing off the saddle before you leave it.

before.rope_note: 4th-class arete/ridge scramble; a short rope may be carried for exposed sections, but many parties solo it unroped.

road.name: Freezeout Ridge Trailhead, via East Chewuch Road / FS-37 / FS-39, north of Winthrop
road.status: Paved/gravel out of Winthrop for the first stretch, becoming rough gravel for the final ~3.2 miles up FS-39 to Freezeout Pass; limited parking at the trailhead.
road.driveNote: Several hours from Seattle via Hwy 20 to Winthrop, then roughly 45 min-1 hour further up the Chewuch River road system.
road.seasonalGate: Snow-free roughly late June through end of September; snowbound/impassable most of the rest of the year

climate.fall: Dry, stable weather early fall (September); rapidly deteriorating by late September
climate.spring: Lower sections may have snow; roads may not be accessible until mid-May
climate.summer: Generally dry rock conditions; occasional afternoon storms; best climbing conditions June-August
climate.winter: Snow and ice on route; not typically attempted
climate.typical: High alpine environment; afternoon thunderstorms common in summer; wind exposure on ridge

waypoints.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
waypoints.note: Follow Trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (~45 min), then traverse south to the base of the North Face.

waypoints.name: Tiffany Mountain
waypoints.note: NE Couloir is a moderate snow/scramble line (low 5th/AI1-2) up the north-facing gully to the summit slope.

climate.fall: Rapidly clearing conditions; window closes by late September as new snow arrives
climate.spring: Heavy snow coverage; roads may not be accessible until May
climate.summer: Snow field conditions June-July; bare by late August; wildflowers peak mid-June through July
climate.winter: Heavy snow accumulation; not typically attempted
climate.typical: High alpine environment with persistent snow into June-July; dry in August-September
